parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what must be changing to induce an e.m.f. - it is not the flux itself but how fast the flux is changing.
Hint 2: Remember to link the size of the induced e.m.f. to the rate of change of flux linkage, using the word proportional for full credit.
parts.proper_answer: The induced e.m.f. is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Faraday tells us**
Think of flux linkage $N\Phi$ as the total magnetism threading the coil. If this stays constant, nothing happens. Only when it changes does the coil respond by generating an e.m.f.

Step 2: **Exact statement**
The size of that effect is set by how fast the change happens: $$E \propto \frac{\Delta(N\Phi)}{\Delta t}$$ In words, the induced e.m.f. is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage. Do not confuse this with Lenz's law, which gives the direction.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
A solenoid S has a small coil C placed near to one of its ends, as shown in Fig. 11.1.
{{figure:figure_11_1}}
Fig. 11.1
The coil C has a circular cross-section of diameter $3.6 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$ and contains 63 turns of wire.
The solenoid S produces a uniform magnetic field of flux density $B$, in tesla, in the region of coil C given by the expression
$$B = 9.4 \times 10^{-4} I$$
where $I$ is the current, in ampere, in the solenoid S.
The variation with time $t$ of the current $I$ in solenoid S is shown in Fig. 11.2.
{{figure:figure_11_2}}
Fig. 11.2

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: there is no electromotive force (e.m.f.) induced in coil C
hints: Hint 1: Since $B \propto I$, the rate of change of flux is zero when the gradient of the current-time graph in Fig. 11.2 is zero - look for the flat tops and bottoms.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link current graph to e.m.f.**
Here $B = 9.4 \times 10^{-4} I$, so flux $\Phi = BA$ follows $I$ exactly. By Faraday, induced e.m.f. $\propto$ rate of change of $I$, which is the gradient of Fig. 11.2.

Step 2: **Find zero gradient**
At the peaks ($t_1$, $t_5$) and troughs ($t_3$, $t_7$) the curve is momentarily flat, so $$\frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} = 0$$ Hence $\Delta \Phi / \Delta t = 0$ and induced e.m.f. $= 0$. Any two of these times is correct.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: the induced e.m.f. in coil C is a maximum but with opposite polarities.
hints: Hint 1: Maximum e.m.f. needs steepest slope on the I-t graph, and opposite polarities need slopes in opposite directions - look where the curve crosses zero going up versus going down.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Steepest slope means biggest e.m.f.**
The magnitude of e.m.f. follows $|dI/dt|$. This is largest where Fig. 11.2 is steepest, which is as it crosses the time axis.

Step 2: **Opposite polarity means opposite slope**
At $t_2$ the current is falling steeply while at $t_4$ it is rising steeply, so $dI/dt$ has opposite signs. By Lenz's law the induced e.m.f. therefore has opposite polarity. So the pair $t_2$ and $t_4$, or the pair $t_4$ and $t_6$, works.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The alternating current in the solenoid S in (b) is replaced by a constant current of $5.0 \text{ A}$.
Calculate the average e.m.f. induced in coil C when the current in solenoid S is reversed in a time of $6.0 \text{ ms}$.
hints: Hint 1: For an average value over a time interval, start from Faraday in the form $E = N\Delta\Phi / \Delta t$ with $\Phi = BA$.
Hint 2: Work out the circular area from the diameter, and note that reversing from $+5.0\text{ A}$ to $-5.0\text{ A}$ means $\Delta B$ is twice the one-sided value.
Hint 3: Convert $6.0\text{ ms}$ to seconds and combine $N = 63$, $\Delta B$ and $A$ to find $E$ in volts.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Set up Faraday for average e.m.f.**
You need magnitude only: $$E = \frac{N\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t} = \frac{NA\Delta B}{\Delta t}$$ where $A$ is the cross-sectional area of one turn of coil C.

Step 2: **Find area and change in B**
Diameter $d = 3.6 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m}$, so $$A = \pi \left(\frac{d}{2}\right)^2 = \pi (1.8 \times 10^{-2})^2 \approx 1.02 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^2$$ Initial $B = 9.4 \times 10^{-4} \times 5.0$. Reversed current is $-5.0\text{ A}$, so change is double: $$\Delta B = 2 \times 9.4 \times 10^{-4} \times 5.0 = 9.4 \times 10^{-3}\text{ T}$$

Step 3: **Calculate E**
Time $\Delta t = 6.0\text{ ms} = 6.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}$ and $N = 63$: $$E = \frac{63 \times 1.02 \times 10^{-3} \times 9.4 \times 10^{-3}}{6.0 \times 10^{-3}} \approx 0.10\text{ V}$$ This is the average magnitude of induced e.m.f. during the reversal.
